title: Substitution, chain rule and first-order Taylor formula for restricted polynomials
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian ring, $I\subseteq A$ an ideal, $r\geq0$, and $P=\widehat{A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]}_I$ [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Use the continuous partial derivatives $\partial_i$ of [def-per-completed-polynomial-conormal]. For every commutative $A$-algebra $D$ complete for $ID$ and every tuple $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in D^r$, polynomial evaluation extends uniquely to an $A$-algebra map $\operatorname{ev}_u:P\to D$ preserving the $I$-adic filtrations; write $f(u)=\operatorname{ev}_u(f)$. Here preserving filtrations means that $I^nP$ maps into $I^nD$ for every $n\geq0$. If $Q=\widehat{A[y_1,\ldots,y_s]}_I$ is $IQ$-adically complete and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_r)\in Q^r$, substitution $\phi_g(f)=f(g)$ satisfies
$$\partial_{y_j}\phi_g(f)=\sum_{i=1}^r\phi_g(\partial_i f)\,\partial_{y_j}g_i$$
for every $f\in P$ and $1\leq j\leq s$; substitution respects identities and composition. Finally, if $D$ is Noetherian, $H\subseteq D$ is any ideal, and $u,v\in D^r$ satisfy $v_i-u_i\in H$, then
$$f(v)-f(u)-\sum_{i=1}^r(\partial_i f)(u)(v_i-u_i)\in H^2$$
for every $f\in P$. No nilpotence of the $u_i$ or $g_i$, and no characteristic assumption on $A$, is required.

source.place: Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), proof Steps 1 and 2, expanded restricted-polynomial calculus; Tag 0AJR (equation-NL), continuous partial derivatives. The square-ideal Taylor assertion makes precise the calculation at the end of Step 2.

proof.text: By [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], $I$ is finitely generated. For any finite tuple of variables $t$, put $S_t=A[t]$ and $P_t=\widehat{S_t}_{IS_t}$. The ideal $IS_t$ is finitely generated by the images of generators of $I$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-module-completion-complete] with ring $S_t$, ideal $IS_t$ and module $S_t$: $P_t$ is complete and separated, and the component $P_t\to S_t/I^nS_t$ is surjective with kernel $I^nP_t$ for $n\ge1$. The module power $(IS_t)^nP_t$ equals $I^nP_t$ since each is generated by products of $n$ elements of $I$. Thus each $f\in P_t$ admits a polynomial $p_n$ with $f-p_n\in I^nP_t$. We use these facts for $P$, $Q$, and later for $\widehat{A[X_1,\ldots,X_r,Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]}_I$.

source.place: Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), Step 1; completion topology justified by algebra.tex Tag 05GG (lemma-hathat-finitely-generated)

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-completed-polynomial-taylor-evaluation] with $T=D$ and $y=u$: it gives a unique continuous $A$-algebra map $E_u:P\to D$ sending each $x_i$ to $u_i$. Every $A$-algebra map $F:P\to D$ preserves the stated filtration: an element of $I^nP$ is a finite sum $\sum_k a_kb_k$ with $a_k\in I^n$, and $F(\sum_k a_kb_k)=\sum_k a_kF(b_k)\in I^nD$. Such a map is continuous. Hence the uniqueness just obtained applies in particular to all filtration-preserving extensions, and $E_u$ has exactly the required properties. The same construction with $D=Q$ and $u=g$ defines $\phi_g$.

source.place: Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), Step 1; Tag 0AK3 (remark-linear-approximation), evaluation map; formal-spaces.tex Tag 0AJM (remark-universal-property)

proof.text: The continuous derivatives supplied by [lem-per-completed-polynomial-taylor-evaluation] agree with those in [def-per-completed-polynomial-conormal]. Indeed, they are $A$-linear extensions of polynomial differentiation. An $A$-linear map sends $I^nP$ into $I^nP$ by the finite-sum calculation of Step 2, so they satisfy the defining uniqueness condition of the latter node. This also applies to $Q$. In particular all these derivatives preserve the filtration and obey the Leibniz rule. Write $\partial_i$ for the common operators.

For a polynomial $p=a\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i}$, the Leibniz rule from Step 3 gives $\partial_{y_j}(a\prod_i g_i^{\alpha_i})=\sum_{i:\alpha_i>0}\alpha_i a\,g_i^{\alpha_i-1}\prod_{k\ne i}g_k^{\alpha_k}\,\partial_{y_j}g_i$. By the monomial formula of [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative], this is $\sum_i\phi_g(\partial_i p)\partial_{y_j}g_i$, the zero-exponent terms being zero. Add over the finite monomial expansion in [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. This proves the chain identity on polynomials even when the $g_i$ are completed polynomials.

source.place: Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), Step 1, verification that the induced arrows form a map of complexes

proof.text: For general $f\in P$ and $n\ge1$, take $p_n$ from Step 1. By Steps 2 and 3, $\partial_{y_j}\phi_g(f)-\partial_{y_j}\phi_g(p_n)\in I^nQ$ and $\phi_g(\partial_i f)-\phi_g(\partial_i p_n)\in I^nQ$. Multiplying the latter differences by the fixed $\partial_{y_j}g_i$ stays in $I^nQ$. The chain identity for $p_n$ from Step 4 therefore makes the difference between the two proposed sides for $f$ lie in $I^nQ$ for every $n$. Separatedness from Step 1 makes that difference zero. Identity substitution fixes every variable, so it is the identity by the uniqueness in Step 2. For a third complete completed-polynomial ring $R$ and tuple $h\in R^s$, both $\phi_h\phi_g$ and $\phi_{(\phi_h(g_i))_i}$ are continuous $A$-algebra maps out of $P$ sending $x_i$ to $\phi_h(g_i)$; Step 2 makes them equal. This proves compatibility with composition.

source.place: Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), Steps 1 and 2, chain rule and compatibility with composition

proof.text: To justify Taylor expansion for an arbitrary ideal, first work in the polynomial ring $U=A[X_1,\ldots,X_r,Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]$ of [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. For a monomial $a x^\alpha$, multiplying the finite factors in $a\prod_i(X_i+Z_i)^{\alpha_i}$ gives terms $a c_{\alpha,\beta}X^{\alpha-\beta}Z^\beta$ for $0\le\beta\le\alpha$, where $c_{\alpha,\beta}=\prod_i\binom{\alpha_i}{\beta_i}$ is an integer acting by repeated addition. The $\beta=0$ term is $aX^\alpha$; the terms $|\beta|=1$ sum to $\sum_i(\partial_i(a x^\alpha))(X)Z_i$ by [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. Thus the polynomial Taylor remainder consists exactly of the terms with $|\beta|\ge2$.

source.place: Tag 0AK3 (remark-linear-approximation), details of the term-by-term expansion omitted in the source

proof.text: For each $\beta$ with $|\beta|\ge2$, list its indices in increasing order with repetitions, and call the first two $i(\beta),j(\beta)$. Place the term $a c_{\alpha,\beta}X^{\alpha-\beta}Z^{\beta-e_{i(\beta)}-e_{j(\beta)}}$ into $L_{i(\beta),j(\beta)}(a x^\alpha)\in U$, and set all other contributions to zero. Extend additively over monomials of $p\in A[x]$. These are $A$-linear maps $L_{ij}:A[x]\to U$, and the preceding finite expansion reads $$p(X+Z)-p(X)-\sum_i(\partial_i p)(X)Z_i=\sum_{i,j}Z_iZ_jL_{ij}(p).$$ Their $A$-linearity implies $L_{ij}(I^nA[x])\subseteq I^nU$ for every $n$: apply $L_{ij}$ to a finite sum of coefficients in $I^n$ times polynomials. No division or characteristic restriction occurs.

source.place: Tag 0AK3 (remark-linear-approximation), explicit grouping of the quadratic and higher terms into the ideal generated by the products of increments

proof.text: Put $R=\widehat U_I$, complete by Step 1. Each $L_{ij}$ induces $L_{ij,n}:A[x]/I^nA[x]\to U/I^nU$. These maps commute with quotient reduction because both orders send the class of $p$ to the class of $L_{ij}(p)$. If $f=(f_n)_n\in P$, the family $(L_{ij,n}(f_n))_n$ is therefore an element $\widehat L_{ij}(f)\in R$ by [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Step 2 provides evaluations from $P$ to $R$ at $X+Z$ and $X$. Choose $p_n$ from Step 1. The polynomial identity of Step 7, reduced modulo $I^nR$, is exactly $$f(X+Z)-f(X)-\sum_i(\partial_i f)(X)Z_i=\sum_{i,j}Z_iZ_j\widehat L_{ij}(f)$$ modulo $I^nR$: evaluations and derivatives preserve the filtration by Steps 2 and 3, and $\widehat L_{ij}(f)$ has component $L_{ij,n}([p_n])$. Equality of all components makes this an exact equality in $R$.

source.place: Tag 0AK3 (remark-linear-approximation), convergence made explicit by compatible polynomial quotients, with the completion defined in formal-spaces.tex Tag 0AL0 (remark-I-adic-completion-and-restricted-power-series)

proof.text: Put $z_i=v_i-u_i\in H$. Apply the evaluation map $R\to D$ of Step 2 at $(X,Z)=(u,z)$ to the exact identity of Step 8. Its composites with the evaluations $P\to R$ at $X+Z$ and $X$ send $x_i$ respectively to $v_i$ and $u_i$, so uniqueness in Step 2 identifies them with $E_v$ and $E_u$. The derivative term similarly becomes $(\partial_i f)(u)z_i$. The remainder is now the finite sum $\sum_{i,j}z_iz_j E_{(u,z)}(\widehat L_{ij}(f))$, which belongs to $H^2$ since each $z_i,z_j$ belongs to $H$. This proves the asserted Taylor formula. In fact this argument does not need the additional Noetherian hypothesis on $D$, which the statement retains. For $r=0$ the sums are empty and all evaluations coincide by Step 2; if $s=0$ there is no chain-rule index $j$. No argument requires any coordinate to be nilpotent.

source.place: Tag 0AK3 (remark-linear-approximation), error in the ideal generated by products of increments; Tag 0GAE (lemma-NL-up-to-homotopy), final calculation of Step 2
